title: Κάμηλος καὶ ἐλέφας καὶ πίθηκος
titleEn: The Camel, the Elephant, and the Monkey
part: The Camel, the Elephant, and the Monkey (Chambry 145)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 145. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων βουλευομένων βασιλέα ἑλέσθαι, κάμηλος καὶ ἐλέφας καταστάντες ἐφιλονείκουν, καὶ διὰ τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ σώματος καὶ διὰ τὴν ἰσχὺν ἐλπίζοντες πάντων προκρίνεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Tōn alogōn zōiōn bouleuomenōn basilea helesthai, kamēlos kai elephas katastantes ephiloneikoun, kai dia to megethos tou sōmatos kai dia tēn ischyn elpizontes pantōn prokrinesthai.
sentences.l: The speechless animals taking counsel to choose themselves a king, a camel and an elephant, having presented themselves, kept contending, hoping, both on account of the size of their body and on account of their strength, to be preferred above all.
sentences.i: When the brute beasts were taking counsel to choose a king, a camel and an elephant came forward and fell to wrangling, each hoping to be preferred above all the rest for his bulk and his strength.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute opens the fable, as it so often does here. ἄλογα ζῷα are animals "without λόγος", and λόγος is both reason and speech — the Greek does not choose between them. ἑλέσθαι is the aorist middle of αἱρέω: the middle is the regular voice for choosing a man for oneself, electing him. καθίστημι in its intransitive aorist (καταστάντες) is to take one's stand, to come forward as a candidate. προκρίνομαι takes the genitive of those one is preferred over. ἐφιλονείκουν is imperfect: the wrangling went on and on.

sentences.t: Πίθηκος δὲ ἀμφοτέρους ἀνεπιτηδείους εἶναι ἔφη, τὴν μὲν κάμηλον, διότι χολὴν οὐκ ἔχει κατὰ τῶν ἀδικούντων, τὸν δὲ ἐλέφαντα, ὅτι δέος ἐστὶ μὴ χοιρίδιον, ὃ δέδοικεν, ἡμῖν ἐπιτιθῆται.
sentences.tr: Pithēkos de amphoterous anepitēdeious einai ephē, tēn men kamēlon, dioti cholēn ouk echei kata tōn adikountōn, ton de elephanta, hoti deos esti mē choiridion, ho dedoiken, hēmin epitithētai.
sentences.l: But a monkey said that both were unfit — the camel, because she has no bile against wrongdoers; and the elephant, because there is fear that a piglet, which he dreads, may set upon us.
sentences.i: But a monkey said neither would do: the camel because she has no gall against wrongdoers, the elephant because there is the fear that a piglet — the very thing he dreads — may come at us.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ separates the two candidates and takes each in turn. χολή is bile, and Greek puts anger there: to have no gall is to be incapable of the anger a ruler needs against the unjust. δέος ἐστὶ μή with the subjunctive (ἐπιτιθῆται) is the regular way of naming a fear of what may yet happen — μή here is "lest", not "not". δέδοικεν is a perfect with present force, "he stands in dread". The elephant's terror of a squealing pig was a commonplace in antiquity. ἡμῖν, "on us", quietly counts the monkey in among the animals he is advising.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλοὶ καὶ τῶν μεγίστων πραγμάτων διὰ μικρὰν αἰτίαν κωλύονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti polloi kai tōn megistōn pragmatōn dia mikran aitian kōlyontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that many are kept from even the greatest undertakings on account of a small cause.
sentences.n: κωλύομαι takes the genitive of what one is kept from. καί goes with τῶν μεγίστων, "even the greatest". αἰτία is the ground or reason for a thing; the point is the disproportion between the size of the beasts and the smallness of what disqualifies them.
